evidence.claim: A desert road through red sandstone and Civilian Conservation Corps history
evidence.quote: CCC workers built campgrounds, trails, stone visitor cabins, ramadas, and roads.

evidence.claim: Valley of Fire Road approaches the park on two lanes through open desert, then takes a hillier, curving course through the Muddy Mountains.
evidence.quote: the two-lane highway travels southeasterly about seven miles (11 km) through open desert terrain towards the Muddy Mountains. The road begins to follow more a more hilly and curvaceous path as it meanders through the mountains.

evidence.claim: The 10.5-mile section between the park entrances became a Nevada Scenic Byway in 1995.
evidence.quote: A 10.5-mile (16.9 km) section of the Valley of Fire Road—the portion between the west and east entrances to the state park—was designated a Nevada Scenic Byway on June 30, 1995.

evidence.claim: Nevada State Parks highlights red Aztec sandstone among gray and tan limestone, petrified trees and petroglyphs more than 2,000 years old.
evidence.quote: 40,000 acres of bright red Aztec sandstone outcrops nestled in gray and tan limestone, Valley of Fire State Park contains ancient, petrified trees and petroglyphs dating back more than 2,000 years.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps crews began work here in 1933, building roads alongside campgrounds, trails and stone visitor cabins.
evidence.quote: Work on the park was initiated by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1933. During their employment, which continued into the early 1940s, CCC workers built campgrounds, trails, stone visitor cabins, ramadas, and roads.

evidence.claim: By 1941, State Route 40 had shifted onto an unimproved alignment through the park’s southern side, resembling the present road.
evidence.quote: By 1941, SR 40 was moved to a new alignment that resembles the present-day alignment of the Valley of Fire Road—the new routing was an unimproved, 23-mile (37 km) roadway traversing the southern side of the Valley of Fire State Park.

evidence.claim: Paving followed by 1964; by 1982, the road no longer carried a state route number.
evidence.quote: The road was finally paved by 1964.

evidence.claim: From the Interstate 15 end, the route heads southeast toward the west entrance.
evidence.quote: The western terminus of the Valley of Fire Road is at the Interstate 15 (I-15) exit 75

evidence.claim: Beyond the fee station it crosses the southern part of the park, passing trails, campgrounds and the visitor center.
evidence.quote: Beyond the fee station, Valley of Fire Road traverses the southern reaches of the state park, passing nearby to various campgrounds, trails, the visitor center, and other points of interest.

evidence.claim: Elephant Rock marks the east-entrance end of the scenic section; the road continues to Northshore Road in Lake Mead National Recreation Area.
evidence.quote: before passing the east entrance station near Elephant Rock, where the scenic byway designation ends. The roadway reaches its eastern terminus two miles (3.2 km) east of there, at an intersection with Northshore Road within the Lake Mead National Recreation Area

evidence.claim: by 1982, the road no longer carried a state route number.

evidence.claim: Nevada State Parks identifies carvings by the Basketmaker culture about 2,500 years ago, followed by the Early Pueblo culture.
evidence.quote: The most obvious evidence of occupation is the petroglyphs carved into the rocks by the Basketmaker culture about 2,500 years ago, followed later by the Early Pueblo culture.

evidence.claim: Paiutes were living in the area in 1865 when Mormons settled at nearby St. Thomas.
evidence.quote: Paiutes were living in this area in 1865 when Mormons settled at nearby St. Thomas

evidence.claim: The rock art and other traces of occupation are protected by state and federal law.
evidence.quote: All artifacts and other signs of early civilization and recent history are protected by state and federal law.

evidence.claim: The park closes to all visitors December 1–14 each year.
evidence.quote: Each year, Valley of Fire State Park closes to visitors from December 1 through December 14.

evidence.quote: The park also preserves three stone cabins built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.claim: Park creation began with the transfer of 8,760 acres of federal land to Nevada in 1931.
evidence.quote: The creation of Valley of Fire State Park began with the transfer of 8,760 acres (3,550 ha) of federal land to the state of Nevada in 1931.

evidence.claim: Crews started in 1933 and worked into the early 1940s, building visitor cabins, roads, trails and campgrounds.
evidence.quote: Work on the park was initiated by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1933. During their employment, which continued into the early 1940s, CCC workers built campgrounds, trails, stone visitor cabins, ramadas, and roads.

evidence.claim: The park opened in 1934, a year before its official designation by the state legislature.
evidence.quote: The park opened in 1934; it achieved official designation by the state legislature in 1935.

evidence.quote: Topographic relief is modest as the summit rises 120 feet (37 meters) above the Valley of Fire Road

evidence.claim: Its Aztec Sandstone began as desert dunes that hardened into rock.
evidence.quote: Elephant Rock is composed of Aztec Sandstone which formed as lithified sand dunes in a desert

evidence.claim: Runoff drains east toward Lake Mead through Thomas Wash and Valley of Fire Wash.
evidence.quote: Precipitation runoff from the landform drains east to Lake Mead via Thomas Wash and Valley of Fire Wash.
